# Simplot Company Secures Agricultural Research & Commercial License from Corteva Agriscience™, Broad Institute of MIT & Harvard
August 06, 2018
BOISE, Idaho, Aug. 6, 2018 /PRNewswire/ -- The J.R.
Simplot Company announced today that it has executed a joint intellectual property licensing agreement with Corteva Agriscience™, Agriculture Division of DowDuPont™, and the Broad Institute of MIT and Harvard for foundational CRISPR-Cas9 and related gene editing tools.
The technology provides Simplot with another avenue to bring desirable traits forward in certain fruits and vegetables and advance products to the market in the United States to benefit both farmers and consumers.
Simplot provides a full line of fresh, frozen and chilled offerings that include potatoes, avocados and strawberries.
Each year, 35 percent of fresh potatoes worth $1.7 billion are lost because of waste from poor storage or shelf life according to the Journal of Consumer Affairs.
Avocados, strawberries and other fruits and vegetables have similar losses and gene editing technology like CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing tools may be able to reduce that significantly.
Using gene editing technology such as CRISPR-Cas9, bruising and browning of potatoes can be reduced, eliminating some of the 3.6 billion lbs. of potato food waste each year.
"We're excited to add CRISPR-Cas9 technology to our platform of tools aimed at providing more sustainable produce for the industry," said Susan Collinge PhD, Vice President of Simplot Plant Sciences.
"These pioneering tools may enable growers to achieve higher yields on less land resulting in fewer pesticides, water and labor needs while extending the quality of a consumer's favorite foods."
Comprehensive intellectual property rights allow entities to apply scientific tools as widely as possible.
To enable such access, Corteva Agriscience™ and Broad Institute have agreed on a joint non-exclusive licensing framework for agricultural use.
The license to Simplot represents the first time that Corteva Agriscience™ and Broad Institute have jointly provided a license of CRISPR-Cas9 genome editing tools to an agricultural company.
...

Using different genetic techniques, the company previously commercialized two generations of its Innate®-branded line of potato varieties by adapting genes only from wild and cultivated potatoes.
The potatoes feature reduced bruising and black spots, reduced natural asparagine and protection from late blight pathogens.
"Our goal is to maximize the scientific impact of CRISPR-Cas9 for improving agriculture, and our joint licensing agreement offers the opportunity to provide much broader access to help researchers reduce food waste, limit pesticides, and improve drought resistance, while promoting safe and ethical uses of groundbreaking technologies," said Issi Rozen, Chief Business Officer of the Broad Institute.

BOISE, Idaho -- An Idaho company that successfully brought genetically modified potatoes to the market announced an agreement Thursday to help a California-based plant breeding company grow strawberries they say will stay fresh longer and have a longer growing season.

Simplot Co. and Plant Sciences Inc., both privately held companies, said they expect to launch the first commercially available, gene-edited strawberries within a few years.

"It's the same technology we're working on with potatoes," said Doug Cole, director of Marketing and Biotech Affairs at Simplot.
"We have the opportunity to do that with this technology."
...
Steve Nelson, president and chief executive officer of Plant Sciences Inc., said the company over the past 35 years has developed five distinct breeding populations of strawberries that do best in various growing areas and climate types.
"They possess complex genomes that contribute to long and complex breeding cycles," Nelson said.
"You've got to look at large populations of seedlings on an annual basis to make progress with traditional plant breeding."
Gene editing could speed that up.
Nelson said the goal of the partnership with Simplot is to improve the horticultural performance of strawberries, enhance pest and disease tolerance and resistance.
...
Simplot, a multinational agribusiness company with headquarters in Boise, Idaho, in 2018 acquired gene editing licensing rights in an agreement with Corteva Agriscience and the Broad Institute of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology and Harvard University, developers of a gene-editing technology called CRISPR-Cas9.
Simplot was the first agricultural company to receive such a license.
The technology allows scientists to make precise changes to the genome of living organisms and has wide-ranging applications for improving plant food production and quality.
It's been likened to using a search-and-replace function while editing a written document.
The gene editing technology speeds up the traditional process of breeding generation after generation of plants to get a certain desirable trait, saving years in developing new varieties that are as safe as traditionally developed varieties, scientists say.
Craig Richael, director of research and development at Simplot, said the strawberry genetic code has been mapped, but it's not clear what traits are associated with all the various parts of the code.
He said the company is working with parts of the code that are known, raising genetically modified strawberries at a Simplot greenhouse.
Plant Sciences Inc., based in Watsonville, Calif., and its affiliates have proprietary rights for more than 50 strawberry and raspberry varieties.
The company supplies plants to growers in more than 50 countries.
Simplot and Plant Sciences will make money by selling the genetically modified strawberry plants to growers, who pay a royalty for the rights to grow and sell the strawberries.
Terms of the deal weren't released.

hits.title: Daily Agri Updates - October 12, 2026
hits.snippet:
## Simplot’s Gene-Edited Strawberry Lines Clear Key UK Precision Breeding Regulatory Step
J.R.
Simplot Company has achieved a major regulatory milestone in England, where eight of its gene-edited strawberry lines have been confirmed as “precision bred organisms” by the Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra).
Developed using CRISPR-Cas9 technology, the strawberry plants feature edits to the *Terminal Flower 1* (*Tfl1*) gene, which effectively removes the genetic brake on flowering to confer remontancy—enabling continuous fruiting across an extended growing season.
Because the edits involved precise native modifications and left no foreign DNA or Cas9 machinery behind, the lines qualify under England’s Genetic Technology (Precision Breeding) Regulations 2025 rather than restrictive transgenic GMO frameworks.
Simplot confirmed that the targeted changes remained stable over three vegetative generations without unintended off-target disruptions, verified using PCR and nanopore sequencing.
The milestone clears the path for planned field selection trials and sensory taste testing across England to ensure fruit quality and flavour remain uncompromised.
Subject to concluding the registration process and clearing the UK Food Standards Agency’s safety review, commercial distribution is targeted across England, Wales, and Scotland.

hits.title: Gene-Edited Strawberries From Simplot Clear UK Regulatory Hurdle
hits.snippet:
# Gene-Edited Strawberries From Simplot Clear UK Regulatory Hurdle
**10 October 2026, England:** Idaho-based food and agriculture company J.R.
Simplot has used gene editing to create strawberry plants that keep fruiting over a longer stretch of the growing season, and the lines have now cleared an early regulatory step in England that moves them closer to field trials and eventual sale.
The UK’s Department for Environment, Food and Rural Affairs (Defra) published a marketing notice on August 21, 2026, confirming eight Simplot strawberry lines as “precision bred organisms” under England’s Genetic Technology (Precision Breeding) Regulations 2025.
That law is separate from, and considerably lighter-touch than, the European Union’s rules for genetically modified organisms.
It allows gene-edited crops to reach the market without the years-long dossier required for conventional GMOs, provided the edits only create genetic changes that could, in principle, have arisen through natural breeding or conventional mutation, rather than inserting foreign DNA.
The trait Simplot engineered is called remontancy, a breeding term for a plant’s ability to flower and fruit repeatedly through the season instead of producing one concentrated harvest.
Many wild strawberries and some breeding lines are naturally remontant, and commercial strawberry breeders have long sought ways to extend the fruiting window without sacrificing fruit size or quality.
Simplot’s approach targets a single gene, Terminal Flower 1 (Tfl1), which in many plants acts as a brake on continuous flowering.
Switching it off removes that brake.
...
## How the edit was made
According to the Defra filing, Simplot used CRISPR-Cas9, the gene-editing tool that works like a pair of molecular scissors guided to a precise spot in the genome, to knock out one or more copies of the Tfl1 gene across eight strawberry lines (identified in the filing as S4A-115, S4A-210, S4A-293, S4A-334, S4A-336, S4A-444, S4A-448 and S4A-480).
Commercial strawberries are octoploid, meaning they carry eight copies of each chromosome rather than the two most crops have, so disabling a trait reliably usually means editing multiple gene copies at once.
In one of the eight lines, S4A-210, the parent plant carried seven copies of Tfl1, and the editing process altered all seven, through a mix of small deletions of one to four base pairs, one 15-base-pair insertion, and a handful of single-letter substitutions.
Notably, every piece of inserted genetic sequence came from the strawberry’s own genome rather than from another species, which is part of why the edits qualify under the UK’s precision breeding framework rather than being treated as a conventional transgenic GMO.
...
## Live Newsroom
The editing tool itself was delivered using Agrobacterium, a soil bacterium long used in plant science to carry genetic material into cells, but only to express the CRISPR components temporarily.
No Cas9 gene or other foreign DNA was left behind in the final plants once the editing was done, a method often called transient expression.
Simplot then verified, across three generations of vegetative propagation (strawberries are typically grown from runners and plantlets rather than seed), that the edited Tfl1 sequences stayed stable and that no unintended changes had crept into the rest of the genome.
That verification used standard PCR testing alongside nanopore sequencing, a newer DNA-reading technology that can scan long stretches of genetic code relatively cheaply, to cross-check the results.
...
## Path to market
The Defra notice itself does not name an individual scientist; it is a regulatory filing rather than a scientific paper, and the company is the named applicant.
Simplot has said it plans line-selection field trials in England during 2026, including taste testing to make sure the extended fruiting trait has not come at the cost of flavor, a common trade-off breeders watch for with remontant varieties.
Commercial marketing is planned for England, Wales and Scotland once the lines complete the registration process, though they would still need to clear the UK Food Standards Agency’s food-safety review before reaching supermarket shelves.
